blocks.prompt: Read this out loud
blocks.text: You have muscles. They are inside you. Make a fist. Bend your arm up. Feel the bump on top. That bump is a muscle. It got short and fat. Now let your arm down. The bump goes soft. Muscles pull your bones. They pull when you run. They pull when you smile. Even your heart is a muscle. It squeezes all day long.

blocks.prompt: Taking Turns
blocks.text: Muscles cannot push. They can only pull. That sounds like a problem. How do you push a door open if muscles only pull? Here is the trick. Muscles come in pairs. One muscle pulls your arm up. The other muscle pulls it back down. Each one takes a turn. The muscle on top of your arm is called the biceps. It pulls your hand toward your shoulder. The muscle under your arm is called the triceps. It pulls your hand back down. Try it. Bend and straighten. Two muscles, taking turns, all day long.

blocks.prompt: Three Kinds of Muscle
blocks.text: Your body runs on more than six hundred muscles, and they do not all work the same way. The ones you think about are called skeletal muscles. They are attached to your bones by tough cords called tendons. When you decide to kick a ball, your brain sends a signal down a nerve, and the muscle pulls. You are the boss of these muscles. The second kind is smooth muscle, and you are not the boss of it at all. Smooth muscle lines your stomach and your gut. It squeezes food along in slow waves while you are busy thinking about something else. It works while you sleep. The third kind is cardiac muscle, and there is only one of it. Your heart. Cardiac muscle never gets a day off. It squeezes about one hundred thousand times a day, and it has been doing that since before you were born. Here is the strange part. Not one of those muscles can push. A muscle has exactly one move: it gets shorter and pulls. Everything your body does, every step and every heartbeat, is built out of pulling.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Muscles pull by sliding threads past each other
Every joint is run by an opposing pair

blocks.prompt: One Move, Repeated Forever
blocks.text: Make a fist and bend your arm. The bump that rises on top is your biceps, and it just did the only thing a muscle knows how to do. It got shorter. That is the whole trick. Muscles pull. They never push. A muscle is a bundle of long fibers, and inside each fiber are two kinds of thread lying side by side. The thick threads have tiny arms along them. When a signal arrives from your brain, those arms reach out, grab the thin threads, and haul them inward, like a crowd of people pulling a rope hand over hand. The threads slide past each other, the fiber shortens, and your arm bends. Multiply that by billions of threads and you get a body that can climb a tree. But if muscles only pull, how does your arm ever straighten again? It cannot push itself. So muscles work in pairs that face opposite directions. Your biceps pulls your forearm up. Underneath it, your triceps pulls your forearm back down. One pulls while the other relaxes, then they swap. Almost every joint in your body is run by a pair like this, taking turns. The muscle does not grab the bone directly. It hands the job to a tendon, a cord tougher than rope, anchored into the bone itself. Your Achilles tendon, just above your heel, is the thickest one you have. Every time you push off to run, you are really pulling on it.

notes: A motor unit is one nerve plus its squad of fibers

blocks.prompt: Delicacy Is Arithmetic
blocks.text: Somewhere between six hundred and eight hundred muscles are wrapped around your skeleton right now, depending on how you count them, and together they make up roughly forty percent of your body. That is not an accident of design. Movement is expensive, and your body has committed more of itself to movement than to anything else. A muscle contracts because a nerve tells it to. But a nerve does not speak to one fiber at a time. A single motor nerve branches out and controls a whole squad of fibers, called a motor unit, and when that nerve fires, every fiber in the squad contracts together, completely. There is no half effort at that level. A fiber is either on or off. The way your body lifts a feather without crushing it is by switching on only a few small motor units, and the way it lifts a heavy box is by recruiting hundreds of large ones at once. Delicacy is not gentleness. It is arithmetic. The fibers themselves are not all alike. Slow-twitch fibers are packed with mitochondria and stained dark by a red oxygen-holding protein called myoglobin. They contract without much force but keep going for hours, which is why the muscles that hold you upright are full of them. Fast-twitch fibers contract hard and fast and quit early. Every person carries a mix of both, and training gradually shifts what those fibers are good at. Muscles also do something you rarely notice. They make heat. Contraction is wasteful, and most of the energy escapes as warmth rather than motion. That waste is a large part of what holds you near ninety-eight degrees. When you get cold, your brain orders your muscles to contract uselessly, fast and small, purely to generate heat. You call that shivering. Use them and they thicken. Ignore them and they vanish. Astronauts on the space station lose muscle so quickly in weightlessness that they exercise more than two hours a day just to arrive home able to stand. Your muscles are not equipment you own. They are a running negotiation with what you actually do.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Actin and myosin slide, they do not shrink
Calcium uncovers the landing sites
Myosin needs ATP to let go, not to grab
Rigor mortis: muscle that cannot release
Satellite cells donate nuclei to growing fibers
Every joint trades force for speed

blocks.prompt: One Move: The Engineering of a Human Muscle
blocks.text: A muscle has exactly one move. It shortens. It cannot lengthen itself, it cannot push, and it cannot hold a position without spending energy. Every human motion, from a sprint to the flicker of an eyelid, is assembled out of that single crude verb: pull. Understanding the body means understanding what has to be engineered around one motion to build a life out of it. Zoom into a muscle far enough and the mystery gets smaller rather than larger. A muscle is a bundle of cells called fibers, and each fiber is packed with parallel filaments of two proteins. Actin filaments are thin. Myosin filaments are thick, and studded along their length are thousands of hinged heads. When a nerve signal reaches the fiber, calcium floods in and uncovers landing sites along the actin. The myosin heads swing forward, latch on, and lever backward, dragging the actin past them. Then they release, cock, and grab again, further along. The filaments do not shrink. They slide. The fiber gets shorter because two sets of ropes are being hauled past each other by millions of tiny hands, and each hand spends one molecule of ATP per stroke. That last detail explains something grim and clarifying. Myosin needs ATP not to grab but to let go. When an animal dies and ATP production stops, the heads stay latched and the body locks rigid. Rigor mortis is not muscle tensing. It is muscle unable to release. Because pulling is the only move available, the skeleton has to supply everything else. Bones act as levers, joints as fulcrums, and muscles are arranged in opposing pairs so that the pull of one undoes the pull of the other. Your biceps flexes the elbow. Your triceps extends it. Neither can reverse itself, so the pair covers both directions. This arrangement also costs you leverage. Your biceps attaches to the forearm only a few centimeters from the elbow, which means holding a five kilogram weight in your hand demands far more than five kilograms of force from the muscle. The body trades force for speed on purpose. A small, slow contraction close to the joint becomes a large, fast movement out at the hand. That is a design decision, not a flaw. Training exploits a second feature. Heavy work damages fibers slightly, and the repair does not merely restore them. Nearby satellite cells fuse into the damaged fiber and donate their nuclei, expanding the fiber's capacity to manufacture protein. The fiber thickens. Notably, you do not grow many new fibers. You grow the ones you already have. Those donated nuclei appear to persist long after a muscle shrinks from disuse, which is part of why someone returning to training after years away regains size faster than a beginner earns it the first time. The muscle keeps a record. None of this makes muscle a possession. Skeletal muscle is metabolically expensive and the body audits it constantly. Stop loading it and it is quietly disassembled within weeks, its protein withdrawn for use elsewhere. Astronauts in orbit lose it fast enough that exercise on the International Space Station is not recreation but medical necessity. The rule underneath all of it is unsentimental. Your body maintains the amount of pulling power your life demands, and not one gram more.
